title: How to Negotiate with Banks on REO Properties: A Step-by-Step Investor Guide
excerpt: REO properties can be some of the best deals in real estate — if you know how to negotiate with banks the right way. This guide breaks down exactly how to approach asset managers, craft winning offers, and close deals at a discount.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: how to negotiate with banks on REO properties
metaDescription: Learn how to negotiate with banks on REO properties. Get step-by-step strategies, offer tips, and scripts to land deep discounts on bank-owned real estate.

sections.content: Bank-owned properties — also called REO (Real Estate Owned) properties — are one of the most overlooked opportunities in real estate investing. When a homeowner defaults and the bank takes the property back through foreclosure, the bank becomes a motivated seller. Banks are not in the business of owning homes. They want to move these assets off their books as quickly as possible, which creates real leverage for savvy investors. If you want to build a pipeline of discounted deals, understanding how to negotiate with banks on REO properties is a skill worth mastering. For a broader look at finding discounted properties across all seller types, check out the [How to Find Motivated Sellers: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/finding-motivated-sellers) — it's a great companion resource to this article.
What Is an REO Property and Why Do Banks Sell at a Discount?

An REO property is a home that a lender — usually a bank or credit union — has reclaimed after an unsuccessful foreclosure auction. If no one bids high enough at the courthouse steps to cover the outstanding loan balance, the property reverts to the lender. At that point, the bank must manage, insure, maintain, and pay taxes on the home. Every month it sits on their books costs them money. Large banks can have hundreds or thousands of these properties at any given time. That carrying cost pressure is exactly why many banks are willing to negotiate below market value.
Step 1: Find the Right REO Properties Before You Negotiate

You cannot negotiate a deal you do not have. REO listings are often posted on bank websites, the MLS, HUD Home Store, Fannie Mae's HomePath portal, and Freddie Mac's HomeSteps platform. You can also find REO leads by monitoring foreclosure filings in your county — which sometimes turn into REO opportunities. Resources like [pre-foreclosure lead lists](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/pre-foreclosure-lead-lists) can help you get ahead of the curve before a property officially hits the REO stage. Active markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) often have a steady flow of REO inventory worth tracking.

Set up automated alerts on HomePath, HomeSteps, and your local MLS for bank-owned properties in your target zip codes. The fastest investors get the first call with the asset manager — and speed matters more than almost anything else in REO deals.
Step 2: Understand Who You Are Actually Negotiating With

When you buy an REO property, you are not negotiating with a grieving homeowner or a landlord — you are negotiating with an asset manager. Asset managers are bank employees or third-party contractors hired to liquidate foreclosed properties. They have performance metrics, approval chains, and internal pricing guidelines. They cannot always make decisions on the spot. Understanding this dynamic is the foundation of every successful REO negotiation. Treat them like a business partner, not an adversary. Be professional, responsive, and organized. Asset managers deal with dozens of investors weekly and will prioritize buyers who make their job easier.
Key Things Asset Managers Care About

items: Clean, all-cash or pre-approved offers with proof of funds
Fast closing timelines — typically 10 to 30 days
Minimal contingencies, especially no financing or inspection contingencies when possible
As-is purchase agreements with no repair requests
Investors who are responsive and close when they say they will
Buyers who do not renegotiate after the contract is signed

sections.content: Step 3: Run Your Numbers Before You Make Any Offer

Never walk into an REO negotiation without knowing your maximum allowable offer (MAO). Banks will sometimes counter above your number, and if you have not done the math, you may overpay and kill your profit margin. Start with the after-repair value (ARV) of the property — what it will be worth after renovations. Then subtract your estimated repair costs, your desired profit margin, and your holding and closing costs. Use the free [Deal Calculator at aiwholesail.com](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to run these numbers quickly and see exactly how much you can offer before the deal stops making sense. A common investor rule of thumb is to offer no more than 70% of ARV minus repairs, but REO deals often allow for even more aggressive offers depending on how long the bank has held the asset.
The bank is not your enemy — they are a motivated seller with a balance sheet problem. When you solve their problem cleanly and quickly, you both win.
Step 4: Craft a Strong Initial Offer

Your first offer sets the tone. Start below your MAO — typically 10% to 20% below what you are willing to pay — to give yourself room to negotiate upward without overpaying. Banks will often counter, especially on newer listings. However, if a property has been sitting for 90 days or more, your initial offer can be much more aggressive. Include a personal letter of introduction, proof of funds (a bank statement or hard money lender letter works), and a clean purchase agreement marked 'as-is.' Some investors also attach a simple one-page deal summary showing their comps and repair estimates to demonstrate they have done their homework. This builds credibility with the asset manager.
What to Include in Your REO Offer Package

items: Completed purchase and sale agreement (use the bank's preferred form when available)
Proof of funds or pre-approval letter
Short bio or company profile showing your track record
Comparable sales (comps) supporting your offer price
Estimated repair budget with contractor quotes if possible
Proposed closing date — 14 to 21 days is ideal for cash offers
Earnest money deposit of 1% to 2% of the offer price

sections.content: Step 5: Navigate the Counter and Close the Deal

Banks rarely accept first offers. Expect at least one counter. When the counter comes in, do not panic — this is normal. Review the counter against your MAO and decide how much room you have. If the counter is within your numbers, accept it quickly. If it is above your MAO, you can counter again with solid data to back your position. Use your repair estimates, comparable sales, and days on market as leverage. Phrases like 'Based on the current condition of the property and recent comps in the area, our highest and best offer is X' work well. Avoid emotional appeals — asset managers respond to data, not stories. If the deal truly does not pencil out, be willing to walk away. The discipline to walk away from a bad deal is what protects your business long-term.

If you are new to REO deals and want to build your negotiation skills faster, study how banks respond to offers in your specific market. Keep a log of your offers, the bank's counters, and final accepted prices. After 10 to 15 deals, you will start to see patterns that give you a major edge.
Common Mistakes Investors Make When Buying REO Properties

items: Submitting offers without proof of funds — banks will not take you seriously
Including too many contingencies, which signals inexperience
Failing to inspect the property before making an offer (not after)
Underestimating repair costs on distressed properties
Renegotiating after the contract is signed — this can get you blacklisted by asset managers
Not having your financing or cash ready to close on time
Ignoring title issues that are common with REO properties — always get title insurance
